A2.text: Six times over. A rich child has a much better chance to enter Taiwan's excellent top school than a poor child ever does. Let's really ask why.
A2.authored_by: Claude (English teacher role), drafted directly (Gemini quota exhausted for this session)
A2.basis: New mission, no workbook source; written per docs/plans/new-mission-playbook.md, angle distinct from sdg1 (general safety-net framing) and sdg1-2 (labor-market framing): social mobility and scholarships specifically. Facts and sources: NTU economics department study using national tax records for the 1993-1995 birth cohort found a child from a rich household is about six times more likely to be admitted to NTU than a child from a poor household; NTU/public-university students' median household income (NTU >NT$1.5M, other public universities >NT$1M) far above the overall sample median (~NT$860,000), producing a 'reverse redistribution' effect since elite public universities receive more government funding per student (報導者/The Reporter coverage of the NTU study, also covered by 商業周刊/今周刊). Stars Program (繁星計畫): multi-track admission by in-school standing rather than only national exam score, designed to widen access for rural/under-resourced students. Ministry of Education's University System Financial Aid Program for Disadvantaged Students (大專校院不利處境學生助學計畫), since the 2007 academic year, targets households in the bottom 40% of income distribution with four kinds of support: tuition subsidy, living stipend, emergency relief, housing subsidy (教育部圓夢助學網/coloan.moe.gov.tw). Early-intervention argument sourced to 獨立評論 commentary on rural education and poverty.
